newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's peso -- heading into trouble?.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's peso -- heading into trouble?.

text.p: Is Mexico's peso heading for a fall?

U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch thinks so. He stirred up a hornet's nest of reaction when he said this week that Mexico was heading for a repeat of its disastrous 1994 devaluation by letting the peso become overvalued.

"There was a problem last time and they didn't listen and there is going to be another problem this time if in the next months they don't start moving towards a real exchange rate policy," Reforma newspaper quoted him as saying at a seminar in the resort of Cancun.
The comments, from a man who correctly predicted the 1994 peso crash, come at a delicate time.
The peso has barely moved in nominal terms in a year. The most-watched 48-hour contract was trading Wednesday at 7.52 to the dollar, against 7.49 a year ago.
Because of Mexico's high inflation -- about 30 percent over the past 12 months -- this has meant a substantial appreciation in real terms.

Voices in the key export sector, in brokerages and in politics are starting to be heard urging central bank Banco de Mexico to nudge the peso down to avoid a loss of competitiveness and a swing back into the red on the trade balance.

Export growth has slowed sharply as the peso appreciates. In August, total exports grew 10.1 percent over the same month in 1995 -- their lowest growth since July 1993, according to Interacciones brokerage.
The head of the Finance Committee in Mexico's Congress, Francisco Suarez Davila, told Reuters a "yellow warning light is flashing" over the peso because of its gain in value.

Yet many analysts here say the peso is not overvalued at its current levels. They are more concerned about what would happen if the currency continues appreciating at its present pace and then trips over.

Using a base year of 1990, independent economist Jonathan Heath said his calculations showed the peso to be 3.3 percent undervalued at the end of August, compared to a trough of 28.2 percent undervalued in March of last year and a peak of 34 percent overvalued in February 1994.

"The peso is probably now about where it should be," he said. "But the exchange rate is not the problem. The real problem is the structural problem of the balance of payments which means that even with a huge devaluation like we had in 1994/5, imports only fell back slightly."

Heath says that unless Mexico tackles its chronic dependence on imports to feed its large "screwdriver" exports of assembled goods, balance of payments problems are likely to reemerge -- regardless of the exchange rate.
The government is standing firmly behind its free market line, insisting that debate about a "correct" level for the peso is futile in a free-floating exchange regime.
One senior government source, speaking on condition he not be identified, told Reuters Dornbusch's assertion the central bank was intervening to keep the peso high was "a lie".

"If Banco de Mexico were intervening to maintain a certain exchange rate, you could argue about whether the peso was over- or undervalued," he said. "But in an absolutely free market, the peso's level is dictated by supply and demand."

But some economists say that although the bank may not have intervened by selling dollars on a large scale, it has influenced the peso's strength by keeping interest rates higher than they might otherwise need to be.
Dollar returns on Mexican Cetes in the first half of this year have been over 30 percent a year -- a big incentive for hot foreign money.

The bank's own report on monetary policy to Congress, issued at the end of September, says that the peso's stability in the first eight months of this year "has been the result of market behaviour". It then adds:

"However, that does not mean that on some occasions Banco de Mexico does not try to influence, through its posture on monetary policy, both interest rates and the exchange rate. This (is) with the objective of helping to achieve the inflation goal and to order prevailing conditions in the exchange and money markets".
The United States, which had to bail Mexico out last time it got its sums wrong on the peso, has kept publicly silent on the delicate issue of the peso.

But U.S. officials have privately expressed concern about whether the peso will be able to achieve a soft landing over the next few months from its current firm levels towards what they term more realistic levels of below 8.20 to the dollar by the year end.
